Definition: Percentage of individuals who used the internet (from any location, via any device) in the last three months. This measures actual internet adoption beyond network availability, capturing the combined effect of infrastructure, affordability, digital literacy, and relevance.
revision_notes: Confirmed. World Bank data (via TradingEconomics) show 11.08% of the population used the internet in 2023. DataReportal's Digital 2024 report corroborates this with 11.3% penetration as of January 2024. Both figures sit well within the <15% bracket (code 1).
revised_comments: Internet usage in Burundi remains very low. World Bank data show 11.08% of the population used the internet in 2023, rising only marginally to about 11.3% by January 2024 according to DataReportal's Digital 2024 report, placing the country firmly in the under-15% bracket.

Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
revision_notes: The cited source itself reports 6.91 kbit/s per internet user (ITU data, 2016), which falls in the 5-19 kbit/s bracket (code 2), not the <5 kbit/s bracket (code 1) that was recorded against it. No more recent ITU per-internet-user bandwidth breakdown for Burundi could be found; 2016 is the last year in that series. A 2025 industry report (ts2.tech, citing a 2019 World Bank digital economy assessment) cites per-capita international bandwidth of only ~591 bits/second, but that figure uses total population rather than internet users as the denominator, so it is not directly comparable to the metric this variable tracks. Given the underlying data is a decade old and the two available metrics point in different directions, this correction should be checked by a reviewer.
revised_comments: International bandwidth per internet user in Burundi stood at 6.91 kbit/s in 2016, the most recent year for which ITU-sourced per-user bandwidth data is publicly available, placing the country in the low (5-19 kbit/s) bracket. As a landlocked country, Burundi depends on cross-border terrestrial fibre links via Rwanda and Tanzania to reach the EASSy and SEACOM submarine cable systems, with the domestic backbone's design capacity further upgraded in 2023.

Definition: Percentage of national population with access to electricity (grid or off-grid). This is the primary indicator of energy infrastructure availability for ICT. Based on World Bank/IEA Tracking SDG7 data, national statistical offices, or Afrobarometer surveys.
revision_notes: Confirmed. World Bank data show 11.6% of the population with access to electricity in 2023, consistent with the <25% bracket (code 1).
revised_comments: Access to electricity in Burundi remains extremely limited, at 11.6% of the population in 2023 according to World Bank data, among the lowest electrification rates in the world.

Definition: Frequency and severity of power outages experienced by businesses and households. Based on World Bank Enterprise Surveys, Afrobarometer, or national utility data. Reflects the quality of electricity supply beyond mere access — critical for running ICT equipment and data infrastructure.
Value Name: Severe (frequent daily outages or regular load shedding)
revision_notes: Confirmed. The most recent published World Bank Enterprise Survey outage-frequency figure remains the 2014 round (16.6 outages/month on average; the original comment's figure of 15 is a close approximation from the same survey). A 2025 Enterprise Survey was fielded (April-August 2025) but its aggregate infrastructure indicators had not yet been published at the time of checking. Numerous 2024-2025 news reports (SOS Médias Burundi, AFP via Punch) document an intensifying national power crisis, including near-daily outages, formal load shedding and a multi-day nationwide blackout in August 2025, supporting continuation of the 'Severe' rating.
revised_comments: Power supply in Burundi is severely unreliable. The last published World Bank Enterprise Survey recorded an average of around 16.6 outages per month for firms, and reporting through 2024-2025 describes a worsening national power crisis, including near-daily outages, formal load shedding and prolonged multi-day blackouts affecting the capital, Bujumbura, and several provinces.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
revision_notes: Confirmed. World Bank data show urban electricity access of 65.0% versus rural access of 2.3% in 2023, a gap of roughly 62.7 percentage points, consistent with the >60pp bracket (code 1).
revised_comments: The urban-rural electrification gap in Burundi is very wide. World Bank data for 2023 show 65.0% access in urban areas compared with just 2.3% in rural areas, a gap of roughly 63 percentage points.

Definition: The number and activity level of technology hubs, incubators, accelerators, and co-working spaces focused on technology and innovation. These provide physical infrastructure and support for tech entrepreneurship and skills development.
revision_notes: The original code of 1 (None identified) rested on a 2019 AfriLabs-Briter Bridges report that did not list any Burundian hub. AfriLabs' current hub directory lists four member hubs in Burundi (Burundi Business Incubator, Maison de l'Entrepreneur, DICOS Incubator, Impact Hub Bujumbura), and further search identifies additional active hubs/incubators outside the AfriLabs network, including BujaHub, KIT-HUB, the Burundi Innovation Hub (BiHUB, an ITU WSIS Prize winner in 2023) and Kesho Innovation Center. This places the country in the 3-9 hubs bracket (code 3) rather than 'none identified'.
revised_comments: Burundi has a small but growing tech hub and incubator ecosystem. AfriLabs' directory lists four member organisations in the country — Burundi Business Incubator, Maison de l'Entrepreneur, DICOS Incubator and Impact Hub Bujumbura — alongside independent initiatives such as BujaHub, KIT-HUB, the Burundi Innovation Hub (BiHUB, an ITU WSIS Prize winner in 2023) and Kesho Innovation Center, together representing regular hub activity within the 3-9 hub range.
